enso.headline: A very strong El Niño keeps building, and it could become the strongest on record this fall.
enso.readingNote: above normal in the key Niño-3.4 zone of the Pacific, latest weekly reading in NOAA's Oct. 19 update
points: NOAA gives a greater than 83% chance of a strong-to-very strong El Niño through January–March 2027, and an 83% chance it beats every El Niño since 1950 this October–December.
Forecasters expect it to keep strengthening through the end of 2026 and to last into spring 2027.
NOAA's winter outlook (Oct. 15) favors a warmer-than-normal winter for the Midwest and drier than normal for parts of the Great Lakes, which often means less snow for La Porte, though not every time.
Around the world, strong El Niños tend to bring heavy rain to parts of South America and East Africa, and drought to parts of Australia, Indonesia, southern Africa and the Amazon.

climate.headline: The climate is warming. Here's what that means, calmly.

points.fact: 2024 was the warmest year on record so far, and the ten warmest years on record have all come in the last decade.
points.doThis: Heat is the deadliest kind of weather in the U.S. Know the signs of heat illness and check on neighbors during heat waves.

points.fact: A warmer atmosphere holds more moisture, so heavy downpours are getting heavier, including in the Midwest.
points.doThis: Know if your home or road floods, keep gutters and storm drains clear, and never drive through water over the road.

points.fact: El Niño on top of a warmer baseline makes new global heat records more likely in 2026 and 2027.
points.doThis: Expect more extremes, not just warmer days: have a basic kit ready and more than one way to get warnings.

sources.label: WMO: State of the Global Climate
